entry.title: Antonelli takes stunning Monza win from 19th on grid
entry.body: Antonelli takes stunning Monza win from 19th on grid - Published Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli took a breathtaking victory in an incident-packed Italian Grand Prix from 19th place on the grid. The Italian caught and passed his team-mate George Russell, who started second, with three laps to go to extend his championship lead to 66 points. Antonelli's performance is the second furthest back a driver has ever come from to win a grand prix after John Watson's victory from 22nd on the grid in the 1983 United States Grand Prix West. It was a statement performance from Antonelli, who remarkably was on Russell's tail and challenging for victory within 16 laps of the start. Antonelli looked capable of winning any which way, but decided to stop for fresh tyres under a virtual safety car mid-race and narrowed a 15-second gap to nothing before carving past Russell. The Italian fans, who usually support Ferrari, rose to acclaim their new hero after a sensational drive as he crossed the line to take the chequered flag. "I did not expect," Antonelli said. I am so happy, I could never imagine being here today." Red Bull's Max Verstappen took the final podium place ahead of the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri. The key stories of a gripping race at Monza were: - Antonelli's compelling and spectacular win, the best of a stand-out season from the Italian - A desperately disappointing day for Russell, who knew he needed to try to use this day to make up points on his team-mate - A disappointing home race for Ferrari, with Lewis Hamilton finishing sixth and Charles Leclerc crashing out early - A good recovery from McLaren Antonelli again comes out on top of Mercedes battle The day started with Antonelli looking to limit the damage inflicted on his points lead by Russell as he started at the back of the grid because of a penalty for using more than his permitted number of engine parts. An early stint of cautious, measured attacking lifted Antonelli up to 12th place on the third lap when Leclerc lost control at the Parabolica after getting slightly wide defending from Piastri, smashing deep into the barriers and bringing out the red flag. Leclerc was unhurt and the race was stopped while the marshals rebuilt the barriers at the famous final corner. By this time, Russell had taken the lead from shock pole winner Pierre Gasly's Alpine and looked in control of the race. But the restart saw a compelling series of laps as the leading drivers ran nose to tail and Antonelli picked his way through the pack and into contention. Four laps after the restart, Russell was leading a six-car train with Antonelli at the rear. Gasly started to drop back and the Italian moved past the Frenchman, Hamilton and finally Piastri before joining a three-car battle for the lead with Verstappen. The Dutchman briefly took the lead from Russell on lap 11, before the Briton re-passed him three laps later, Antonelli overtaking the Red Bull into the second chicane. From laps 17 to 24, the Mercedes battled hard, the two passing and re-passing each other as they played with the boost and overtaking modes in the new hybrid engines as Verstappen sat right behind them with the best seat in the house. Antonelli was then told that Russell had been asked to push and build a gap to Verstappen, and the tension was betrayed in Antonelli's response, when he asked if they wanted him to sit back and not challenge. Shortly afterwards, a virtual safety car was called when Lance Stroll's Aston Martin broke down at the first chicane and Antonelli's side of the garage decided to risk a stop for fresh tyres. Russell stayed out, needing to nurse his tyres to the end, and Verstappen followed Antonelli in. Antonelli rejoined in sixth place and 15 seconds behind his team-mate, but he moved past Gasly, Norris, Hamilton and Piastri as he closed in on his team-mate. Russell began to struggle with his tyres as Antonelli homed in and by lap 48, with five to go, the two were nose to tail. An initial attempt into the first chicane on lap 50 came to grief when Antonelli got on to the rubber debris off line turning into the second part of the first chicane and slid into the gravel. But such was his pace advantage that he soon closed the 1.7-second gap that had opened up and easily breezed past Russell on the run between the Lesmo corners and Ascari. A resigned Russell said: "When I looked at the leaderboard a few laps after the restart and saw he was already in P5/6 I knew he would be in the mix. I was just struggling with the tyres at the end. It has been more positive than before summer break but of course I would have loved to be P1 today." Leclerc shattered by error as crash follows Hamilton contact Ferrari's day to forget started when Leclerc barged Hamilton on to the grass exiting the first chicane on the opening lap, the seven-time champion dropping to 10th. Leclerc then challenged Gasly for third on lap two before being passed by Verstappen into Ascari. That slowed his exit, and left him vulnerable to Piastri, who attacked on the inside into Parabolica. Leclerc was slightly wide on entry and through the apex, and that carried his left rear tyre wide onto the white line on the edge of the track, and partly over the artificial grass section before the gravel trap. There, the car lost grip, and a high-speed tank-slapper spun Leclerc into the barrier at high-speed. After climbing from the car, he sat down behind the barriers, his head bowed, shattered by his error. Hamilton recovered well initially, with a strong restart moving him up to fourth within two laps. But the Ferrari's lack of straight-line speed was ultimately costly and he slipped behind Antonelli and the McLarens as the race wore on. Verstappen impressive as Norris gets Piastri at end Everyone was put in the shade by Antonelli's superlative drive, but Verstappen was impressive in moving up from sixth on the grid to third in the Red Bull and fighting for so long with the Mercedes. In the end, he could not hold on to the silver cars and his stop drop him behind Piastri, Hamilton and Norris. His fresher tyres helped him move back into third place but he could go no further. Behind him, Norris began to move up as the race went on, and he passed Hamilton before moving on to the back of a three-car train behind Verstappen and Piastri. Norris looked to make a move on Piastri in the closing laps but the Australian eased him over to the grass on the outside of the exit of Curve Grande as Norris went for the inside approaching the second chicane. Norris complained he had been pushed off, and the team warned Piastri to race clean, but Norris finally did make it past on the final lap. Gasly was never going to hold on to the lead, and the Alpine's lack of pace after his stunning qualifying performance, aided by compromises elsewhere, soon began to tell. But seventh is a good result as Alpine went into the race aiming mainly to ensure they finished ahead of the Racing Bulls, their rivals for fifth in the constructurs' championship. Gasly succeeded, but Arvid Lindblad beat the second Alpine of Franco Colapinto to eighth place as the second Racing Bulls driver Yuki Tsunoda completed the top 10. entry.title: Red Sox Place Ceddanne Rafaela On 10-Day IL - MLB Trade Rumors
entry.body: The Red Sox have placed center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela on the 10-day injured list (retroactive to Sept. 3) and recalled infielder/outfielder Nate Eaton from Triple-A Worcester, the team announced. Rafaela is dealing with a right quadriceps strain. Rafaela, who missed Boston’s previous three games, will be eligible to return Sept. Whether that happens will depend on the severity of the strain, but the Red Sox will have to go at least a week without another of their top position players. They were already down first baseman Willson Contreras, who has been on the IL with a hamstring strain since Aug. Thanks in no small part to Rafaela’s efforts, the Red Sox will enter Sunday’s series finale in Baltimore at 78-65 and in firm control of a Wild Card spot. Rafaela and Contreras are tied for the team lead in fWAR (3.9), the same total the former posted during a breakout showing in 2025. Over 569 trips to the plate, Rafaela has slashed .282/.317/.443 (108 wRC+) with 16 home runs and 17 stolen bases. The 25-year-old Rafaela has combined quality offense with superb work in center, where he won a Gold Glove in 2025 and may do so again this season. He has accounted for 20 Defensive Runs Saved and 15 Outs Above Average and Fielding Run Value apiece. Rafaela is top seven among all major leaguers in each of those three categories, including a second-place tie with Yankees left fielder Cody Bellinger in DRS. Rafaela only trails teammate and right fielder Wilyer Abreu (25) in that department. Rafaela has sat out just five games since the beginning of June. The Red Sox started Eaton in center in one of those contests and used trade deadline acquisition Eli White for the rest. White will start there Sunday as the Red Sox go for a four-game sweep against the Orioles.

entry.title: Vardy joins Burnley on season-long contract
entry.body: Ex-Leicester striker Vardy joins Burnley - Published Former Leicester City and England striker Jamie Vardy has joined Burnley until the end of the season. The 39-year-old, who is Leicester's record Premier League scorer with 145 goals, departed for Cremonese in 2025. Vardy left the Italian side in the summer and now joins the winless Clarets who are bottom of the Championship. "This club has a proper footballing history and passionate fans who deserve a team that represents them and their town," Vardy told the club website., external "I can't wait to get going on the pitch and help the team move in the right direction." Vardy, who won 26 caps for England, scoring seven goals, spent 13 years at Leicester after signing from non-league Fleetwood Town in 2012. He went on to score 200 goals in all competitions in 500 appearances. Burnley, relegated from the Premier League last season, have made a poor start back in the second tier and have not won in five matches under new boss Nicky Hayen. On Saturday they conceded two goals in the final 10 minutes to lose 2-1 at home to Bristol City. entry.title: McColgan wins London Big Half after five months out
entry.body: McColgan wins London Big Half after five months out - Published Eilish McColgan claimed her fourth victory at the Big Half in London on Sunday after returning to action following five months out with a broken toe. The 35-year-old Scot suffered the injury during the London Marathon in April, crossing the line in seventh place with blood seeping through her shoe, and was forced to pull out of July's Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. But McColgan showed the benefit of a month of warm weather training, completing a comfortable victory over the 13.1-mile course back in the English capital. "I haven't even run 13 miles in training! I have mentally ticked that box and can push on from here, which is great," said the British women's half-marathon record holder. - McColgan might have 'one more' Games in her - Published29 July - McColgan to miss Glasgow Games defence after foot fracture - Published25 July She beat last year's winner Jessica Warner-Judd by one minute 19 seconds, finishing in a time of 1hr 10mins 54secs. It was more than three minutes outside her best time for the course and well outside her British record for the distance of 1:05:43. But McColgan added: "I came into this race in a different place from previous years, coming back into training for the last four weeks, so fitness was always going to be my biggest concern. "I had fear over the broken toe, [so] I eased into it because of nerves and could really attack in the second half." Britain's Jack Rowe missed out on a record fourth consecutive victory in the men's race, finishing in second place, 14 seconds behind Birchfield Harriers' Kadar Omar Abdullahi, who won in a time of 1:01:51. Britain's David Weir defended his title in the men's wheelchair event, winning the race for the fifth time in its nine-year history in a new record time. The 47-year-old, who retired from Paralympic competition in 2024, knocked 45 seconds off his own record for the course, which he set last year, winning in 46:13. Eden Rainbow Cooper won the women's event in 52:47 to defend her title.
entry.summary: Britain's Eilish McColgan returns to competitive action after five months out with a broken toe to win the London Big Half for a fourth time.

entry.title: Wellens wins Tour of Britain as GB's Askey finishes second
entry.body: Wellens wins Tour of Britain as GB's Askey finishes second - Published Belgium's Tim Wellens won the 2026 Tour of Britain as Nils Politt claimed victory on stage five. Wellens began the day with a 21 second lead over Great Britain's Lewis Askey and extended that to 42 seconds as he finished eighth, 21 seconds behind German Politt, on the final stage. Askey finished 40 seconds adrift of Wellens on the 156.1km run through Earlston but managed to hold on to second place, with Belgium's Jasper Stuyven 21 seconds behind him in third place. Great Britain's Elliot Rowe ended the event in sixth place, with compatriots Mark Donovan in ninth and Ben Wiggins in 10th. Prior to the start of the stage, the riders gave Briton Ben Swift a guard of honour as the 38-year-old recently announced he will retire at the end of the 2026 season. Politt launched an attack with just under nine kilometres to go and saw off Wiggins before going on to win his first stage since 2022.
entry.summary: Belgium's Tim Wellens wins the 2026 Tour of Britain as Nils Politt claims victory on stage five.

entry.body: Top-ranked women's player Aryna Sabalenka has cruised into the round of 16 at the US Open and plays again on Sunday against American Taylor Townsend. But in her last match, the Belarusian finally found something that could stop her: the smell of marijuana. Sabalenka said she had never smelled the odor so strong as she did while serving early in the match on Friday, per the AP. "I don't know if it was, like, coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium," Sabalenka said. I just hope they're going to be a bit more aware of that stuff." Sabalenka was serving in the third game of the match in Louis Armstrong Stadium in Queens when she tossed the ball up but then let it fall to the court. She did the same thing on the next point, with something clearly bothering her. She then approached the chair to ask for help. Alas, no fans were found to be smoking. A park located behind the grounds where the US Open is played is one likely source.

entry.title: Kyle Whittingham evaluates Michigan QB Bryce Underwood’s ‘not outstanding’ game vs WMU - Maize n Brew
entry.body: It was a hot start to season for Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood, going 5-of-5 on Michigan’s first drive for 61 yards. Underwood capped off the opening drive with a QB sneak to put Michigan up 7-0. However, Michigan’s offense and Underwood became ineffective up until the last drive of the game. A 47-yard Hail Mary from Underwood to JJ Buchanan gave Michigan a 13-12 win, but Underwood’s performance was largely poor. Kyle Whittingham evaluates Michigan QB Bryce Underwood’s ‘not outstanding’ game vs WMU Here’s what Kyle Whittingham said about Bryce Underwood’s performance against Western Michigan. Underwood threw an interception at the end of the half that netted Western Michigan three points. He also fumbled with two minutes left in the fourth quarter, leading to three more points for WMU. Underwood threw other passes into contested traffic and was fortunate to escape the game with only two turnovers. Underwood acknowledged he “had a few” mistakes “that could have cost” Michigan the game. And while recognizing his play wasn’t up to snuff is a good first step, is there any hope he will improve as a sophomore? After the game, Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham was asked about Underwood’s performance and called it “not outstanding.” Whittingham still held firm that Underwood “improved dramatically” during fall camp. However, Saturday’s showing looked like more of what Underwood has been to this point in his career — inconsistent with sloppy footwork and mechanics. A quarterback who either forces throws or is simply too tentative. “I’m not saying that Bryce played a bad game. This isn’t on Bryce Underwood. It’s on me,” Whittingham said. “And I’ve got to figure out a way to have these guys better prepared and be able to get into a rhythm offensively. It’s like we never got into a rhythm after that first drive. We always found a way to screw it up. We were like 0-of-5 or 0-of-6 before we converted a third down, I believe. And you just can’t win football games like that. We were very fortunate to win, obviously.” Whittingham said he doesn’t talk to Underwood much during games and lets offensive coordinator Jason Beck and quarterbacks coach Koy Detmer Jr. be the ones who are in his ear the most. “Leave that to Jason Beck and Koy Detmer, the voice he hears all week long,” Whittingham said. “And anything from me is just to say, ‘Hey, hang in there, keep competing. You’re our guy,’ and just vote some confidence.” Underwood is Michigan’s ‘guy’, but that could change with other performances that, as Whittingham put it, are not outstanding.
entry.summary: Kyle Whittingham evaluates Michigan QB Bryce Underwood’s ‘not outstanding’ game vs WMU Maize n Brew Michigan wins on second-chance Hail Mary; Big Ten stands by review ESPN Michigan’s controversial win adds to the nagging feeling that college football just isn’t fair CNN Clock controversy allows Michigan Wolverines to avoid massive upset against Western Michigan Fox News Big Ten explains why officials added time to Michigan vs. WMU game The Detroit News

entry.title: ‘I Dream of Jeannie’ actress Barbara Eden, 95, abruptly drops out of film festival - Page Six
entry.body: ‘I Dream of Jeannie’ actress Barbara Eden, 95, abruptly drops out of film festival See more of our coverage in your search results. Add Page Six on Google Actress Barbara Eden abruptly dropped out of appearing at the Cinecon Classic Film Festival due to a “sudden illness.” “We’re sorry to share that, due to a sudden illness, Barbara Eden will no longer be able to appear in person at Cinecon tonight,” event organizers announced on Facebook Saturday. “Barbara is deeply regretful that she had to cancel at the last minute, as she had been very much looking forward to seeing everyone and celebrating with us,” the Cinecon 62 Classic Film Festival team continued. “We know how many of you were excited to welcome Barbara. We appreciate your understanding and join you in sending her our best wishes for a speedy recovery,” they concluded. Though the “I Dream of Jeannie” star, 95, won’t be at the event, the film festival said they will still honor her, as she was set to receive the Cinecon Legacy Award. Eden’s co-star Pat Boone accepted the award on the actress’ behalf. Both Eden and Boone, 92, starred together in “All Hands on Deck” and “The Yellow Canary.” It’s unclear what illness Eden is currently battling. Page Six has reached out to her reps for comment but did not immediately hear back. Eden’s acting and singing career spans over seven decades. Most notably, she starred as Jeannie alongside Larry Hagman as Major Anthony Nelson in the hit NBC sitcom “I Dream of Jeannie.” The hit series spanned 139 episodes across five seasons from 1965 to 1970. In a 2024 interview, Eden opened up about how she has managed to stay in shape over the years. “I used to work out all the time,” she told Fox News at the time. “I used to do spinning classes and then do weights with a trainer. … When COVID hit, that ended my heavy workouts. Now, I have a stationary bicycle, and I lift five pounds. I use very lightweight weights, but they’re good for your bones.” Eden and her husband, Jon Eicholtz, tied the knot in 1991. She shared son Matthew Ansara with her first husband, actor Michael Ansara. Matthew died of a heroin overdose in 2001. Discussions are moderated for civility.

entry.body: Susan Sarandon said she’s “still had movies taken away recently” over her outspoken support of Palestine. At the Venice Film Festival press conference for her new film “The Echo Chamber” on Sunday, Sarandon was asked if she thinks the narrative is changing in Hollywood when it comes to the conflict in Gaza. In 2023, the Oscar winner was dropped by her agency UTA after comments she made at a pro-Palestinian rally and said earlier this year she felt she was shunned by the industry for calling for a ceasefire in Gaza. “I think that the narrative has completely changed in terms of historical relevance of Palestine and the ties of Zionists with America and our politics. entry.title: Wim Wenders Clarifies His Stance on Filmmakers’ Role in Politics After Berlin Controversy: ‘We Are the Opposite of Politicians … We Are the Antidote’
entry.body: Wim Wenders has clarified his much-discussed statement about filmmakers’ role in politics that kicked off a firestorm at Berlin Film Festival earlier this year. Wenders was at the center of a heated debate at the Berlinale in February after the celebrated German filmmaker, who served as jury president, said during the opening press conference that filmmakers “should stay out of politics.” “We have to stay out of politics because if we make movies that are dedicatedly political, we enter the field of politics,” Wenders said at the time. “But we are the counterweight of politics, we are the opposite of politics. We have to do the work of people, not the work of politicians.” Popular on Variety The statement then dominated the discourse at the festival, with nearly every filmmaker and actor facing a question about politics — including the ongoing conflict in Gaza and ICE raids in the U.S. — during their respective press conferences. Author Arundhati Roy even pulled out of the festival in protest, and festival director Tricia Tuttle had to put out a statement in response to the frenzy. Asked to reflect on his statement Sunday during a press conference at Venice Film Festival, where he is presenting his latest documentary “From Inside Out — The Architecture of Peter Zumthor,” Wenders said that he “could repeat the same thing,” though admitted he “could be more explicit.” “What I said then was, as filmmakers, we are the opposite of politicians. Politics work without empathy; that’s all I said,” Wenders, who sported an “Imagine Peace” shirt, began. “We have a very different thing. I’m not working with a mindset of politicians, we are working with a mindset of empathetic people. And we are into changing things, politics are into confirming what is.” He continued, “That’s what I said and was quoted as ‘We have to stay out of politics,’ and that is not what I said, because it’s not what I said now and I said the same thing then. The frame of filmmakers is a different mindset than the mindset of politicians, and we should not work with that mindset. We work with a different set of rules. I said it again, and I hope you’re not misquoting me and say we have to stay out of politics, because we do the opposite. We are the antidote.” At Venice’s opening press conference earlier in the festival, jury president Maggie Gyllenhaal weighed in on the topic, saying that movies are “fundamentally, undeniably political.” “Look, we could say, how are we possibly here talking about movies right now when the world is in a state of emergency?” she said. “To me, the answer has something to do with empathy. I think that film allows an opening into an opportunity to find empathy inside of ourselves.”

entry.title: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Two Married Couples Begin to Covet Each Others’ Lives in the Latest Stunner from ‘Burning’ Director Lee Chang-dong - IndieWire
entry.body: We use vendors that may also process your information to help provide our services. Another heart-stopping and novelistically layered stunner from modern cinema’s most literary auteur (a fiction author himself), Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love” might be dedicated to the memory of Krzysztof Kieślowski’s “Dekalog 10,” but let’s dispel any notion of it being a remake. Conceived independently, and then lumped during pre-production into the same tribute omnibus that kicked off with Asghar Farhadi’s dreadful “Parallel Tales” at Cannes this year this film shares nothing in common with the final episode of Kieślowski’s series beyond the biblical commandment that Lee splays on screen at the very start: “Thou shalt not covet.” And even then, the evidence of that instruction proves elusive in this sprawling drama about two very different couples who are brought together by the violent suppression of a workers’ strike at a major Korean metals factory. Who is coveting what, exactly? It’s simple enough to understand what the film’s characters want on the surface — or at least that’s true of its women. A casually rich dilettante whose pale skin glows with the same lustrousness as her salon-perfect bob, first-time director Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, similarly cast as the rich mom in “Parasite”) hopes to make a documentary about the declining state of labor across South Korea, with a particular focus on the recent unrest at a business called SP Heavy Industries. Although we see Ye-ji pitching the project to a grant board of some kind, the presumption is that most of her funding — and all of her creative freedom — has been provided by her imperiously chiseled husband Sang-woo (Lee newcomer Zo In-sung), a trust fund type who appears to enjoy a rather frictionless existence. On the other side of the economic divide, the plucky but sad-eyed Mi-ok (played by “Secret Sunshine” actress Jeon Do-yeon, who delivers another once-a-century performance less than 20 years since her first collaboration with Lee) is clearly willing to do whatever it takes to bring her husband back to life. One of the “dead” who lost his job and sense of purpose in the mass layoffs at SP two years ago, her taciturn and implosive Ho-seok (“Peppermint Candy” star Sul Kyung-gu) has been a shell of himself since being injured amid the crackdown that ended the ensuing strike, and Mi-ok hopes that participating in Ye-ji’s doc might allow him to process his trauma — to stop shuffling around like a zombie and snap back into the man she once fell in love with as a teenage seamstress who didn’t have any better options. That he might become a more present father to their young son Cheol, whose current rudderlessness is best expressed by his abject incompetence at Taekwondo. Beyond that simple baseline, the matrix of desire at work in Lee and Oh Jung-mi’s remarkably nuanced script is too slippery to pin down until the movie’s velvet gutpunch of a final scene. Yes, Mi-ok lusts after Ye-ji’s elegant wardrobe and designer handbags, and there’s an unspoken sexual charge in the air whenever she’s alone with Sang-woo (a charge that eventually sets fire to an unforgettable pre-dawn sequence on a private beach in the third act). But it would be unwisely reductive to conclude that the working-class woman is jealous of her hyper-affluent new bestie, just as it would be unhelpfully rash to assume that envy plays a more pivotal role in this story than resentment, or that a film as mottled and probing as “Possible Love” might be content to retrench the divide between Korea’s haves and have-nots. Lee is perfectly happy to inflame our anger towards the one percent, and the movie’s jagged script — first inspired by a similar incident at a massive Korean company more than 10 years ago — is at its broadest when poking fun at how blithely Ye-ji inserts herself into Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s blue-collar world. She wants to be a fly on the wall in their downtrodden factory town, but the pampered documentarian stands out like a Maybach at a monastery; despite growing up without a silver spoon in her mouth, she rages at her inability to code-switch back to a lower rung on the financial ladder. As the story goes on and Ye-ji convinces Mi-ok and Ho-seok to join them for a weekend at Sang-woo’s luxurious vacation house along the country’s western coast (all the better to entrap the couple on her turf where she can film them at all hours of the day), Lee finds a devious variety of ways to weaponize the running visual gag in which an intimate scene pans over to find Ye-ji hiding in the corner with her camera. It’s admirable that she wants to highlight how workers are being left behind as the ownership class automates their businesses in order to hoard their wealth, but Ye-ji fails to recognize the many condescending ways that she infringes upon her subjects’ dignity, as if — in a world where labor is increasingly rendered invisible from the people who profit from it — people like Mi-ok and Ho-seok should feel lucky to be seen at all. In contrast to Lee’s monumental and more explosive “Burning,” the story he tells here builds on an instance of terrible violence rather than building to it, but his latest film simmers to a boil at a similar clip, and likewise alternates long dialogue scenes with indelible moments of visual acuity. While it’s hard for this comparatively restrained domestic saga to compete with Jeon Jong-seo’s sunset dance along the DMZ, Lee retains his gift for whipping spectacle out of thin air — for infusing something as routine as a car ride home or a quick dip in the ocean with an overwhelming degree of silent pathos. Every moment in “Possible Love” crackles like a wicked symphony of striated socioeconomic abrasion; every gesture, comment, and detail sharpens the strange geometry that brings these people closer together at the same time as it deepens the divides that will ultimately keep them apart. Sometimes, in a handful of judiciously deployed moments, that geometry is expressed in skin-crawling fashion. Case in point: Sang-woo keeps an antique whistle on the living room mantle of his summer palace, and the resident “house fairy” — a seemingly non-verbal groundskeeper who Sang-woo used to play with when they were kids — is conditioned to come running whenever he blows on it. For the most part, however, the distance between the film’s characters is conveyed in subtler terms; in the confidence of Sang-woo’s upright posture, the brittleness of Mi-ok’s wavy hair, and the brusque impenetrability of Ho-seok’s blank stare, which doesn’t suggest the absence of an inner life so much as it betrays the constant struggle to bottle up his demons. He’s a prisoner of the pain that Ye-ji breezily documents like a tourist. The careful attention that Lee pays to his characters’ bodies and how they wear them pays off — enormously — after “Possible Love” relocates to Sang-woo’s summer home for this 164-minute film’s last hour (“This is like a house from a novel I haven’t read,” Mi-ok gawps over dinner). Between a night of drunken karaoke and a few pre-dawn strolls along the mansion’s private beach, the movie’s financially driven exploration of freedom and power begin to assume a more physical dimension, a transition which threatens to confuse the dynamics that have otherwise tethered everyone to their roles; this is where Jeon seizes control, her raw and marbled performance reaching a state of self-preservation so primal that it renders the rest of the characters senseless. “Possible Love” takes brilliant — if unnerving — pleasure in leveling the playing field between its two couples, but those shifty indulgences are too freighted with reality to feel like wish fulfillment. The film isn’t naive enough to pretend that its “poor” characters might ever achieve true equilibrium with its rich ones, nor is it patronizing enough to suggest that there’s some kind of implicit dignity to being exploited by the carelessness of late capitalism. Ho-seok is not a holy sufferer, he’s a profoundly broken and embittered man whose plight speaks to the hopelessness of fighting back against a system that’s designed to trample people like him, and Lee is far more interested in rendering his pain than he is in “solving” it. The ultimate power of “Possible Love,” which grows in the mind after it’s over (and greatly rewards any repeat viewings), is rooted in neither wanton despair nor false optimism. Despite being steeped in the sadness and frustration of the working class, Lee’s drama uses its film-within-a-film construct to refract the moral valences of labor through the prism of what people actually earn through their work. Slumming it as a documentarian as she builds towards her dream of being a narrative filmmaker (“Imagining things is my hobby” is maybe not what you want to hear from the person directing a documentary about your life), Ye-ji is a victim of her own second-hand affluence — the seamlessness of her life has life has made it so that she has to performatively “method act” in order to get close to her subjects and shoot anything real. Her observational technique is a parody of the invisible labor that she laments noticing the first time during a trip to a luxurious Qattari hotel, but she can’t even see people like Mi-ok and Ho-seok unless she contrives a scenario for them to exist for her camera. For his part, Sang-woo’s work is so frictionless that he can buy and sell entire companies from his laptop while sipping a latte, and his marriage to Ye-ji feels like it’s laminated in plastic. They passively snipe at each other in short bursts so as not to get any dirt on the bedsheets, and relegate all of their latent desires to the blind spots that rich people create so that they don’t have to see the world beyond their own wealth. By contrast, Mi-ok and Ho-seok have no choice but to confront the hardships that have been visited upon them, and to want for things so badly they can never lose sight of the work they’ve put into each other. Their lives are principled upon a possible love, because they don’t have the luxury of pretending there’s any other kind. Yes, their history together — fleshed out in a series of perfectly modulated flashbacks — is clumsy and imperfect, and their financial prospects for the future are tenuous at best, but they will never have to covet what this world still offers to people for free. Mi-ok and Ho-seok have always felt as if the moon shined only for them at night, and the final moments of this gently shattering and astonishingly well-shaded drama exalt in the freedom they give to each other by saving its glow for themselves. “Possible Love” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Netflix will release it in theaters on Friday, October 23, and on Netflix on Friday, November 6.
entry.summary: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Two Married Couples Begin to Covet Each Others’ Lives in the Latest Stunner from ‘Burning’ Director Lee Chang-dong IndieWire Possible Love review – a tale of two couples is finely judged study of exploitation and friendship The Guardian ‘Possible Love’ Review: Korean Master Lee Chang-dong’s Transfixing Meditation on Economic and Emotional Unease Is a Quiet Powerhouse The Hollywood Reporter 'Possible Love' Is a Delicate Drama of Love and Longing in Anxious Times Time Magazine 'Possible Love' Review: Lee Chang-dong's Quietly Colossal New Drama Variety

entry.title: ‘From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor’ Review: Wim Wenders’ Latest 3D Documentary Is an Architectural Marvel
entry.body: The screen is usually a canvas, but it becomes a window to an enormous room in Wim Wenders’ latest 3D documentary, “From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor.” Within that room unfolds the tale of the Swiss architect of the title, told in occasionally laborious ways. It spends much of its two-hour runtime teaching you how to watch it, and like your average high school class, you might not see the value of its instruction until it eventually comes in handy. In that vein, Wenders presents some magnificent things in the film’s final third, sensations which emerge like Zumthor’s own views on the function of his buildings, which he ties to human experience, understood by its inhabitants gradually, and then all at once — from the inside out. Beginning with shots of concave corners and convex, monolithic surfaces, “From Inside Out” engenders curiosity before taking academic detours. These come courtesy of Zumthor himself, whom we first meet as a ghostly projection upon sleek, minimalist surfaces, emanating from the 1980s. Like the Holocaust survivors whose poetry populated the walls in Wenders’ “Anselm” — his 3D retrospective on the works of sculptor Anselm Kiefer — Zumthor’s words become inseparable from each room the camera explores, and each building the architect believes ought to feel at one with its surroundings. Popular on Variety We eventually meet Zumthor in the present: an unassuming man in his eighties, whose descriptions of form, function and fluidity often repeat themselves, but whose sincerity and wisdom are hard to shake. As the film explores houses, museums and other Zumthor commissions, the architect’s use of light and natural materials becomes as important as the theoretical people he intends to fill each space — or, in the case of complicated restorations, the people who inhabited them decades ago. Wenders depicts these ghosts of past and future through dramatizations of curious travelers, whose whispering voiceover offers scattered thoughts on where they stand. There’s a tinge of humor, too, in Zumthor’s stubbornness when designing someone’s home, as the conceptual clashes with the preferential. However, the architect eventually gives way to use and function first, despite valuing the aesthetics at hand (not to mention, his collaborations with local artisans). It isn’t long before Wenders introduces the idea that Zumthor’s spaces are only as important as what goes inside them, when he first contrasts old and contemporary footage of museums he designed, each filled with deeply personal art installations — some of them about war. Zumthor himself doesn’t have the most interesting personal history — at least, not as far as this film is concerned — so Wenders’ exploration can come off as superficial at first. However, this ends up part and parcel of the structure. It echoes the feeling of approaching a marvelous building from afar, and entering its sterile lobby, before slowly discovering its mischievous secrets. Although some scenes and enactments can meander, they give way to a moving triptych of projects whose presentation feels, in a way, climactic. One is a home deeply personal to Zumthor. Another is a Nordic installation built in tribute to women killed in witch trials, which feels terrifying to walk through — a kind of infinitude accentuated by Franz Lustig’s 3D cinematography. And the third is arguably Zumthor’s magnum opus: his sprawling, amoebic construction housing the permanent collection at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, whose planning and completion the doc depicts in detail. By the time the building is finished (and visited by a number of filmmakers, including Ava DuVernay and Werner Herzog), Wenders’ camera moves in tandem with Zumthor’s own abstract notions of the art pieces needing to feel horizontally equal, with none being granted more or less importance than any other. The sprawling gallery seems to have no beginning or end. Its bends extend endlessly, revealing pockets and side rooms with rough, exposed concrete contrasting the gilded grandeur of the pieces on display. It takes a while to realize this, or at least to internalize it, but the film’s own architecture is not dissimilar, with what feels like winding segues that add up to an experience of fluid expanse, of great wandering, and ultimately, of soulful appreciation. Certainly, no one is beholden to a film this demanding, but Wenders wields his 3D camera to craft a perfect marriage of subject and form, filling echoing spaces with art and stories much like Zumthor’s architecture does — until eventually, you leave with a new appreciation of the physical world, and your place within it.
entry.summary: The screen is usually a canvas, but it becomes a window to an enormous room in Wim Wenders’ latest 3D documentary, “From Inside Out – The Architecture of Peter Zumthor.” Within that room unfolds the tale of the Swiss architect of the title, told in occasionally laborious ways. It spends much of its two-hour runtime […]

entry.title: Bob Minkin’s Best Photos of New York Music in the Seventies and Eighties
entry.body: “Those are concerts that I attended. I started the list with my very first show, Eric Clapton at Roosevelt Stadium in 1974. I got home from seeing Frank Zappa at the Palladium, and I duly wrote it down. Show number 73, and it’s a godsend because I can tell you the truth, a lot of those shows on there I have no recollection of.” Albert Collins, Lone Star Cafe, NYC Dec. 5, 1982 “That’s Albert Collins sitting there on top of a car outside of the Lone Star Cafe. I loved him, he was known as the Iceman or the Master of the Telecaster. He would famously wade into the audience, come off the stage and walk through the crowd. in this case though, he actually walked out the front door of a packed place. He’s playing the guitar and one of the guys was trailing his cord out. A bunch of people followed him out the door, including me.” “Every year, the Allman Brothers play a multi-night run at the Beacon Theatre. his was the first time the Allman Brothers Band played at the Beacon. I heard they had a new guitar player, this guy named Warren Haynes. I remember thinking to myself, ‘Man, that guy’s got some big shoes to fill.’ As we know, he filled them quite well.” Brent Mydland, Go Ahead, The Ritz, NYC Sept. 26, 1986 “This was the Grateful Dead’s Brent Mydland’s side band, Go Ahead. For me, seeing a Grateful Dead band member coming to New York at a relatively small venue was exciting for anybody who was into the Dead to see the band members out of character, not at the Brendan Byrne Arena. The drummers and keyboard player got to shine.” Bruce Springsteen, Palladium, NYC Sept. 17, 1978 “I really had no idea of the power of a Bruce Springsteen show [until I attended this show]. People ask me today a lot of times, they know I’ve been to thousands of concerts. ‘What was the best show you ever saw?’ And I said, ‘Well, I can’t really say the best show, but I could tell you one of the best shows I ever saw out of any band was the first time I saw Bruce Springsteen.’ Because he played like his life depended on it, like if he didn’t deliver a good show, he would’ve been tortured to death or something. He played like his foot was on the pedal to the floor. Turn it up, nevermind 11, turn it up to 15.” Buddy Guy, Lone Star Cafe, NYC Nov. 14, 1984 “The shot here of Buddy Guy is taken with a flash because the Lone Star Cafe lighting was not always good. I had to be judicious about shooting because I could I get thrown out of there. But here’s Buddy in a real action pose, and that’s the thing you got to wait for – those moments. I was right in his face with the flash, but it didn’t matter because didn’t bother him. But still, you had to be careful.” Buddy Cage, Lone Star Cafe, NYC March 20, 1984 “So that’s Buddy Cage, the pedal steel guitar player in the New Riders of the Purple Sage. Buddy, he doesn’t normally do that, that’s not part of his routine. So these things happen in a split second, and if I’m just daydreaming or talking to somebody or going to the bathroom [I might miss it]. You had to be ready.” Dr. Pepper Music Festival,Wollman Rink, Central Park Aug. 18, 1978 “So the thing about the Central Park shows were that if you couldn’t get in or if they were sold out, you could listen to it from the surrounding hills around there. Or like this enterprising group of kids did, you can climb up in a tree and then actually watch the show. I just love all their expressions. I think maybe one of them notices me.” Frank Zappa, The Ritz, NYC Nov. 17, 1981 “I love Frank Zappa and this was in ’81, one of the last times I saw him play. Zappa was he was big in my neighborhood [in Canarsie,Brooklyn]. Some of the music was a little far out [for me] as a young teenager. But since all the people who I thought were cool loved Zappa, that means I had to like Zappa too. At the Ritz show here, part of his show is he’s a director. He doesn’t always just up there playing guitar and singing. He has a big band and he directs them, and he talks and tells stories and stuff.” “I can’t believe a show like this even happened. I had access for it, a photo to be upfront. Boy, I wish I had backstage for this show. Just to see David Gilmour playing with Johnny Winter. This was at the end when they all came out at the end to play, but each of them had their own segment, Dickey Betts playing Blue Sky, the Steve Cropper segment doing Green Onions, the Neil Schon segment doing some Journey song, whatever. They had a house band, drummer or bass player, so they would come on and off. Guitar Greats, that’s the least superlative way you can call this thing.” Pictured (L to R): Dave Edmunds,Johnny Winter, Brian Setzer, Dickey Betts, Steve Cropper and Neil Schon. (Link Wray and David Gilmour are hidden). Jerry Garcia Band, Palladium, NYC Nov. 27, 1977 “I was 18 years old when I took this shot. I still was using what’s called a Konica Rangefinder camera — a very affordable, cheap camera back then that a kid like me could have, but you could still take a great photo with it. You’re looking through basically a hole in the camera that has no relation to the lens. The funny thing at this show was I only had like one negative strip from it because I think I went to the show with only one roll of film that was mostly used up. So I only have a handful of shots from this show.” Johnny and Edgar Winter, The Bottom Line, NYC Sept. 5, 1978 “This was billed as a Johnny Winter (left) concert and his brother, Edgar surprised the crowd, performing with his brother for the second half of the show.” Jorma Kaukonen and Jaco Pastorius, My Father’s Place, Old Roslyn, NY Jan 4, 1985 “This photo is of Jorma Kaukonen, from Hot Tuna and Jaco Pastorius, world-renowned bass player, he was in Weather Report. It was crazy music, just avant-garde type stuff. To get a picture like this back then, you could only do this with a flash, and it’s experimental. You don’t really know how it’s going to come out. So what you do is you got to shoot at a slow shutter speed, capture movement. When you fire the flash, that freezes some of the action so everything’s not just a blur. And then I had a zoom lens, so I zoomed the lens during the long exposure. That’s why the trails are coming out.” Jorma Kaukonen and Jaco Pastorius, My Father’s Place, Old Roslyn, NY 1-4-85 Jorma Kaukonen, Lone Star Cafe, NYC Oct 1, 1985 “That’s Jorma Kaukonen at the Lone Star. He played there all the time. For a San Francisco music freak like me, seeing him in my hometown all the time was just great because he moved to the area. He wasn’t in San Francisco anymore. This is from one of his hundred million nights at the Lone Star Cafe. As you could see, I’m shooting him in the dressing room, and it’s a friendly situation because we know each other. So he’s giving me a nice smile.” Ramones, Bond’s International Casino, NYC Feb.20, 1981 “In Times Square, there was this big clothing store that used to be there called Bonds. When clothing store went out of business, somebody came up with the idea to make it into a venue. I can’t really remember what got me to go to this show, but I’m glad it did, because the crowd was packed, and it was mellow.” Robert Hunter and Comfort, Other End, NYC May 12, 1978 “Robert Hunter was kind of the invisible guy in the Grateful Dead. As far as I was concerned, I just saw his name on an album that said, ‘Hunter-Garcia,’ and I really didn’t know what that meant. There was nothing about him because back then you couldn’t look things up. So it was like, Hunter, who is he? And there’s no pictures of him, there was nothing about him anywhere. And then I found out he was going to actually be playing and touring with band was called Comfort. So there he was in the flesh and at The Bitter End.”
entry.summary: Noted music photographer Bob Minkin started going to shows in New York City when he was just 15. Soon after, he was sneaking his camera into venues to document what he saw. The experience led to an assignment to photograph concerts for Relix Magazine while studying graphic design at the School of Visual Arts. His […]

entry.title: Phaedra Parks and ‘Traitors’ co-star Chris ‘CT’ Tamburello make red carpet debut at Creative Arts Emmys 2026 - Page Six
entry.body: Phaedra Parks and ‘Traitors’ co-star Chris ‘CT’ Tamburello make red carpet debut at Creative Arts Emmys 2026 Roll out the red carpet. Phaedra Parks and her former “Traitors” co-star Chris “CT” Tamburello made their red carpet debut at the Creative Arts Emmys 2026 on Saturday. According to photos obtained by Page Six, Tamburello had his arm around the “Real Housewives of Atlanta” star’s waist as they posed together at the award show. Parks, 52, looked stunning in a black velvet dress that featured crystals lined along the cutout portion. Her blond bob was flipped and she paired her look with diamond jewelry. The “Real World” alum, 46, looked dapper in a classic black tuxedo. The couple did not show any PDa on the red carpet. Stay one step ahead with all the exclusive tea on your favorite reality TV stars! Tamburello and Parks’ show, “Traitors,” was nominated for seven Emmys and took home six of them. The outing came two days after the “Married to Medicine” alum confirmed she and the “Challenge” star were dating. Page Six exclusively reported that Tamburello and Parks’ blossoming romance was a long time coming. “He made it clear to her he really, really liked her and he fell for her when they were on ‘Traitors,’” a source told Page Six Friday. We’re told Tamburello recently began to reach out to the mom of two more. “He makes her really happy,” our source added. “They really do laugh together a lot and their relationship is really sweet.” Tamburello and Parks became fan favorites when they appeared on “Traitors” Season 2 together in 2024. At the time, the attorney was one of the secret traitors and was banished by their castmates, while Tamburello went on to win the series. Parks shares sons Ayden, 16, and Dylan, 13, with ex-husband Apollo Nida, from whom she finalized her divorce in July 2017. Tamburello shares son Christopher “C.J.,” 10, with ex-wife Lilianet “Lili” Solares, from whom he divorced in 2022. He then secretly married Catalina Hager in October 2024. The OnlyFans model filed for divorce in January. Discussions are moderated for civility.

entry.title: ‘Father Joe’ Review: Kiefer Sutherland Comes Out With All Guns Blazing - Deadline
entry.body: “This place” is a drug lab, and while Lino is checking out his investment, a man in black starts picking of his crew with the stealth of a ninja and the armory of the Marine Corp. After shooting Lino in the foot, the stranger reveals himself as Father Joe (Kiefer Sutherland), an actual priest who takes on Manhattan’s drug dealers wearing his work clothes. “I’m here to put you back on the right track,” he says, and orders him to confess. Watch on Deadline Being a good Catholic boy, as all mobsters used to be, Lino does so, and Father Joe lets him live on two conditions: One, no selling drugs to kids under the age of 21. “You can’t save everyone,” he reasons, with a strangely beatific smile. The other condition is way more Bessonian: Father Joe injects Lino with a complex homemade virus that will become deadly within seven days.

entry.title: Witkoff and Kushner, in a first, visit Ukraine for peace talks
entry.body: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday for diplomatic talks aimed at resuming negotiations between Russia and Ukraine . Why it matters: Kushner and Witkoff traveled to Kyiv right after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. This is Witkoff and Kushner's first trip to Ukraine despite months of negotiating with both sides and multiple trips to Russia. Sunday also marked the highest-level visit by a U.S. official to Ukraine since Trump started his second term. Driving the news: U.S. and Russian officials offered positive assessments of Kushner and Witkoff's three-hour meeting with Putin on Saturday. "Kushner and Witkoff are making an effort, and we are making progress," a Russian official said. A White House official said Witkoff, Kushner and Putin discussed "plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks." Witkoff, Kushner and their team left Moscow on Saturday night, landed several hours later in Poland, and then traveled by land to Kyiv. Zoom in: Zelensky discussed Ukrainian preparations for continuing the war through the winter, a source familiar with the meetings said. Kushner and Witkoff stressed they want a breakthrough before winter, the source said. Witkoff and Kushner met twice with Zelensky and his senior advisers. National security advisers from the U.K., France and Germany joined a third meeting. After the second meeting with Zelensky, Trump's envoys said they were "encouraged by the substantive discussion" and looked forward to making more progress.

entry.title: Iran warns of 'faster, heavier, more painful response' to US attacks
entry.body: Iran warns of 'faster, heavier, more painful response' to US attacks - Published Iran's top negotiator has warned of "a faster, heavier, and more painful response" to US attacks, as hostilities between the two sides escalate. Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Sunday that Americans must understand "before it is too late" that the "rules of the game have changed", according to a translation of his comments on state media. His comments come nearly a week into renewed fighting between Iran and the US, and a day after Washington said it struck Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran attacking American warships in the region's waters. The BBC has contacted US Central Command (Centcom) for comment. Iranian state media also reported on Sunday that the country's Navy had attacked an American remote-controlled vessel that was trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz. The US military has denied the claim. "The report came from Iranian state media and it's a total lie," said Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Centcom, according to the Associated Press. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has issued his own threats back at Iran, writing on social media on Saturday, "It's simple: if Iran shoots at US ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers." A 60-day ceasefire between the US and Iran formally expired last month, and that period of relative calm was shattered when the US resumed attacks last Sunday. Fighting has continued throughout the week, with the US launching multiple strikes on Iranian targets and Iran retaliating against US targets in the region, including in the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan. US President Donald Trump said this week that the renewed fighting would not last "too long", echoing comments both he and his administration have frequently made since the now six-month-long war began in February. Months of negotiations between the US and Iran have not amounted to lasting peace, and there's little sign of a further diplomatic settlement on the horizon. The Strait of Hormuz, which is crucial to the world's oil and gas industry, has been effectively closed since the war began, and has become a major source of leverage for Iran. Tehran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway. But Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route. The conflict in the strait has led to an increase in gas prices globally, and ahead of the US midterm elections in November, Trump is facing pressure over how much the war is costing American consumers. The average price for one gallon of diesel in the US hit $5.85 on Friday, compared to an average of $3.71 a year ago. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Sunday that an average of 9 million barrels of oil a day were passing through the strait, which could help ease pressure on energy prices. Wright told CNN with oil also moving through pipelines in the region, "we're probably two-thirds or more of pre-conflict flows". In an interview with ABC This Week on Sunday, Wright added that gas prices should start to come down for Americans as summer demand begins to wane after Labor Day. Related topics - Published23 hours ago - Published28 August
entry.summary: The comments came a day after Washington said it had struck Iranian oil tankers in response to Tehran's attacks on US warships in the region.

entry.title: Zelensky says he expects war to continue into winter after talks with US envoys
entry.body: Zelensky says he expects war to continue into winter after talks with US envoys - Published Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said he expects the war with Russia to continue into the winter, following talks with Donald Trump's top envoys in Kyiv. The discussions finished without an announcement of a major breakthrough, after Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travelled to Ukraine for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion. The previous day, the pair had held talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Witkoff said he was "encouraged" by what he called "substantive" and important talks in Kyiv. Zelensky stressed that he wanted a just peace with no opportunity for renewed aggression by Russia. - The 'thorny' issues that threaten to derail a Russia-Ukraine peace deal - Published30 December 2025 Following rounds of talks on Sunday, which lasted several hours behind closed doors, Zelensky told reporters they had agreed officials from Ukraine, Europe and America would meet in the near future to continue discussions. He also called for a trilateral meeting with Russia and the US. "We're confident there'll be a good resolution here," Witkoff said, adding the negotiators had "made a lot of progress in Moscow", referring to the pair's discussions on Saturday. When asked about the talks in Moscow, Kushner said the US team "went through a lot of the ideas that hadn't worked to date" and "tried to think about" what elements are needed for "durable peace". "It was a very good dialogue, he [Putin] asked a lot of questions, we asked a lot of questions." Witkoff said the envoys had met the Russian leader prior to travelling to Kyiv as they "needed to hear where he stood". Zelensky emphasised that should the war continue into the winter - "which is what it looks like for now" - Ukraine would need air defence and energy support. Ukraine has relied on American-made Patriot interceptors to combat Russian ballistic missiles, but the US has used many of its stockpiles during its war with Iran. In past years, Russia has focused its attacks on energy infrastructure during winter months. Zelensky said Ukraine needs to develop its own anti-ballistic system, but added the Americans will be increasing production next year, which they are "counting on". The US envoys had travelled to Kyiv by train after flying to Poland â Zelensky told the media that it was not possible for them to land their plane despite preparations. Putin and Zelensky agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while the negotiators carried out their trip. Zelensky greeted Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's St Sophia Cathedral, near where a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine's security services on Friday. Overnight, Russian and Ukrainian forces continued to exchange strikes, with Ukraine confirming they struck an oil refinery, an airfield, and two air defence systems. Earlier, Ukraine's Air Force reported that Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 long-range drones and small cruise missiles. The country's air defences downed 82 drones and six missiles, but 11 locations were hit, with debris falling at a further seven sites. Saturday's talks in Moscow lasted three hours and were held behind closed doors in the Kremlin, according to Russian state media. Putin's adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "constructive, extremely frank". He said they spoke about resolving the war, economic issues, and potential "mutually beneficial Russian-American projects". Ushakov also said "note was made of the Russian army's tangible advances in the combat zone" and that there was acknowledgement that talks needed to address "the root causes of the conflict". Despite an escalation of Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, Russian ground forces have made very slow advances for most of the conflict, incurring enormous casualties. Russia still controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory â areas that it seized back in 2022. The talks come after Russia and Ukraine have intensified aerial attacks in recent months. - Published2 days ago - Published22 hours ago
entry.summary: There was no announcement of a major breakthrough, after Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travelled to Kyiv.

entry.title: Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority
entry.body: Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority - Published Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) is heading for a big victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals, according to incomplete results. Projections indicate it is set to fall short of a majority, but the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern. The far-right AfD is set to win a record 44% of the vote, well ahead of the conservative CDU on just over 17%. The AfD's charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said it was "sensational" and they wanted to start governing as soon as possible. No far-right party has won control of a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture. Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35. With more than 90% votes in, the AfD is set to score higher than earlier opinion polls suggested, and Siegmund along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as the news emerged. Commentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant. "This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal." US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD". Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference. The AfD's leaders will not know if they have enough seats to govern until they see which of the smaller parties get into the state parliament. Siegmund has so far refused to lead a minority government, but the party's national leaders see it as a possibility. "If necessary there'll just be new elections, then we'd just get 50 or 55%," said Siegmund, while saying he was prepared to work with individual MPs or a party. A big question-mark hangs over whether one populist left-wing party, BSW, gets over the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament. If BSW fails, then the AfD's chances of a majority increase. If they get in, the AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament. A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen. A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem. "We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory and said his party would have to deal with the result: "This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign." Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin" and he was adamant that they would hear it. AfD stands for Alternative fÃ¼r Deutschland and it openly pro-Russia and anti-migration. It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result as well. Although the outcome was initially unclear, the party's supporters believe they are on the march. Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at an estimated 78%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters. One man called Ollie said: "This man gives us what no-one else can give." "No matter what government, they all just promise things to get better. This is a party for the working people. It is the alternative for Germany," he told the BBC. Another AfD voter called Bert said people in the east could sense things were not going well: "Things need to improve for us, for my family - I have three children. I'm in fear, I'm really in fear that safety erodes more and more." Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament. The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states. They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power. Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. It would not be able to achieve either if it ran the government of one of 16 states. But it would have significant local powers. The party has been particularly critical of the Bauhaus school of design which the Nazis shut down in the city of Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt after they came to power in 1933. The AfD has called it "the dead-end of modernism", prompting some to accuse the party of using similar language to the Nazis. Nikita, a demonstrator at an anti-AfD "Democracy Festival" in Magdeburg on the eve of the vote said Germans had to "learn from our history and not go back. We don't want the dark times any more". Responding to the news from Saxony-Anhalt, the veteran head of the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, Charlotte Knobloch, said it frightened her. "On days like this I find it hard to recognise my homeland any more," the 93-year-old Holocaust survivor said, appealing for mainstream parties not to stand by and allow "this decline". One of the AfD's top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, has also been criticised for his approach to Russia. When asked why he had a Russian army mug in his office, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".
entry.summary: Germany's AfD has hailed a "historic result" and is projected to win 44% of the vote, far ahead of the conservatives on 17%.

entry.title: Volcano eruption leaves 170,000 passengers stranded in Indonesia
entry.body: Volcano eruption leaves 170,000 passengers stranded in Indonesia - Published Around 170,000 passengers have been left stranded after a volcanic eruption forced Indonesian authorities to temporarily suspend operations at eight airports. Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport was the first to be closed on Sunday morning after ash from Anak Krakatau was detected in airspace near the airport. The transport ministry said 1,558 flights have been delayed with airports remaining closed until 09:00 local time on Monday morning. The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said. The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur. Transport Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said the decision to temporarily close more airports was made after tests found that volcanic ash had spread towards West Java. He urged airlines to speed up processes for refunding tickets for passengers who have been affected by flight cancellations, and for airlines to provide timely information to those with upcoming flights to avoid overcrowding at airports. According to Indonesia's meteorological agency BMKG, ash reached as far as 20,000ft (6,000m) on Java on east of the volcano, and 50,000ft (15,000m) west of the volcano on the Sumatra side. - Are you stranded due to the eruption? Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra. The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks. According to local newspaper Kompas, several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents reported eye irritations from the ash, while some fishermen had cancelled fishing trips at sea similarly reporting sore eyes. One resident, Aldi Candra Prayogi, told the outlet that he felt since Friday evening and it felt like "small grains of sand had gotten into my eyes", and that he needs to use eye drops to ease the irritation. The dust is so thick that he has to sweep the front yard of his house every five minutes, he also said. Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa. The volcano - also known as Anak Krakatoa - collapsed in December 2018, triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java. Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high. The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand. Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes. entry.summary: More than 170,000 airline passengers are stranded after ash was detected in airspace near Jakarta following the eruptions.

entry.title: Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi - bbc.com
entry.body: Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi A residential building in the Indian capital Delhi has collapsed with dozens of students feared trapped inside. Eyewitnesses told local media that as many as 50 people were inside the five-storey building in the Satya Niketan neighbourhood of south-west Delhi when it came down around 13:30 local time (08:00 GMT) on Sunday. At least three people were killed and three others are in a critical condition, news agency PTI reports, citing local police. At least eight people were said to have been rescued so far, according to reports. There had been construction work going on in the basement of the building, Hostel Daze, which sits a short distance from the Delhi University campus. Many of the students staying there were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday. A legislative assembly member said at the scene that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble. Eyewitnesses told local media that another building beside the hostel had also collapsed. One told news agency ANI that the other building had also been a hostel. Chief Minister of Delhi Rekha Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure". "Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added. Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old. The owner of a nearby shop told ANI that it had been under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to expand the hostel and increase their income. "They strengthened the upper building, but the pillars below were weak," he said, noting that the construction workers had also been buried. The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account. "Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said. Police are searching for the owner of the building, Times of India reports. Satya Niketan is a densely populated area which houses a large student population, with a number of hostels in the neighbourhood. Building collapses are relatively common in Delhi, with more than a thousand recorded in the past three years causing dozens of deaths, according to fire department figures. Poor foundations, inadequate materials and unqualified construction workers were among the common reasons for collapses. Eleven people, including three children, were reportedly killed last April when a residential building collapsed in north-eastern Delhi.

entry.title: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel - bbc.com
entry.body: 140 migrants in single dinghy rescued in English Channel Around 140 migrants in a single dinghy have been rescued in the English Channel. The people on the inflatable vessel, which launched from the Normandy coast overnight, requested help in UK waters and were picked up by two RNLI boats, the French coastguard said. They will now be taken to shore in the UK. It comes days after Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings. In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel. The dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water. It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth. On Sunday night in Portsmouth protesters were involved in a stand-off with police near the Eastney Landing ferry port, where small boat occupants had been brought to shore. French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles away from the usual launches around Calais making the crossing to the UK significantly longer. Last year local officials told the BBC there has been an increase in people trying to depart from Normandy. A Home Office spokesperson said on Sunday: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. "Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election." They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches." In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further. While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies". It's thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area. Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16, 513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

entry.body: AfD celebrate projected win in Saxony-Anhalt Germany's far-right Alternative fÃ¼r Deutschland (AfD) is celebrating as exit polls show they are set to win more than 44% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. entry.title: Amazon-branded cargo plane overruns runway at Miami airport, strikes multiple vehicles - NBC News
entry.body: Five people are dead and five others were injured when an Amazon-branded cargo plane crashed just outside Miami International Airport on Sunday afternoon, officials said. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft overran the runway just before 2 p.m. ET while it was landing, according to officials. The plane, 21 Air Flight 7598, was arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, the Federal Aviation Administration said. The plane overran runway number 30, struck multiple vehicles, and came to rest at a field next to the airport, Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said. Three people are in critical condition and were transported to a trauma center, and another two that were transported to a local hospital, Miami-Dade Fire Chief Raied Jadallah said. A hotline has been set up for family members who may have been involved in the tragedy. Video showed plumes of smoke billowing from the wreckage. Multiple vehicles near the airport were struck, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue. Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel clarified that it was an Amazon flight operated by 21 Air. The company is working to support everyone affected, Nantel added. “This is a fast-moving situation and we’re still gathering details. We’re working closely with local authorities and officials to understand exactly what happened,” she said. “Right now, our absolute priority is the safety, well-being, and care of everyone involved.” All runways and taxiways at Miami International Airport were closed following a ground stop, an airport spokesperson said in a statement. ET, two of the four runways at the airport had reopened, the airport spokesperson said, and the airport was under a ground delay. Fire and rescue personnel responded to the scene “within seconds,” said Miami-Dade County Mayor Daniella Levine Cava. More than 60 Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the scene, where firefighters worked to extinguish a “very complex fire” that involved blazing engine compartments, said Jadallah, the fire chief. A search and rescue operation was also launched to retrieve the pilot and co-pilot, trapped in the plane, he said. The plane struck “a couple of vehicles,” leaving some victims trapped inside and prompting a “a complex extrication” by a technical rescue team, Jadallah said. The National Transportation Safety Board said it is gathering information. The FAA and NTSB will determine the cause of the crash. The NTSB said it has launched a team to investigate the incident.
